reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations
chapter_title: Geomaterial Design Parameters and Geotechnical Reports

sections.title: In-Situ Soil Testing
sections.summary: In-situ tests give soil parameters where undisturbed sampling is difficult and supplement borings. Primary tests: SPT, CPT, CPTu, SCPTu and vane shear; PMT and DMT are used less. All are index tests needing local correlation and laboratory benchmarking. Table 5-1 lists tests per design parameter; Figure 5-1 shows the schematics; Table 5-2 (in 5.1.1) the advantages and disadvantages.
sections.body: (pp. 99-101) Soil, rock and aggressive conditions affect driven pile design; in-situ and laboratory results define properties, often correlated to the primary design parameters, shear strength and deformation (chapter introduction, p. 99; see also AASHTO 2014, Bowles 1992, Mayne et al. 2002, Duncan and Wright 2005 and GEC-5, Sabatini et al. 2002). Table 5-1 lists the field and laboratory tests for each design parameter in cohesionless soil, cohesive soil and rock. In-situ tests give parameters where high quality undisturbed samples cannot be obtained, supplement conventional exploration and help pick strata for sampling; without an adequate program the engineer must be more conservative, which is not recommended. The primary in-situ tests are the SPT, CPT, CPTu, SCPTu and vane shear (VST); the pressuremeter (PMT) and flat dilatometer (DMT) are used less. Each applies a different loading (orientation, strain rate), so all in-situ tests are index tests that need local correlation and, where possible, benchmarking to laboratory tests. Figure 5-1 shows the test schematics; Table 5-2 (printed in Section 5.1.1) summarizes applicability, advantages and disadvantages. NHI course 132031 and Mayne et al. (2002) cover in-situ testing in depth.
key_points: Table 5-1: field and laboratory tests for each design parameter in cohesionless soil, cohesive soil and rock
Primary in-situ tests: SPT, CPT, CPTu, SCPTu and vane shear; lesser used: PMT and DMT
All in-situ tests are index tests that require local correlations; benchmark to laboratory tests where possible
Without an adequate testing program a more conservative, less certain design results (not recommended)
Table 5-2 (printed in 5.1.1) summarizes each in-situ method's use, advantages and disadvantages

sections.title: Standard Penetration Test
sections.summary: SPT (ASTM D1586): 140 lb hammer, 30 in. drop; N = blows for the 2nd and 3rd 6 in. intervals (50/x on refusal). Energy transfer about 45 % donut, 60 % safety, 80 % automatic; calibrate yearly (ASTM D4633); safety hammer N 1.9-2.7 times automatic N (Finno 1989). N60 = N(ER/60) (Eq. 5-1); (N1)60 = Cn N60 (Eq. 5-2), Cn = 0.77 log(40/sigma'vo) <= 2.0 (Eq. 5-3) or (pa/sigma'vo)^n (Eq. 5-4). Table 5-2 summarizes the in-situ methods.
sections.body: (pp. 102-109) The SPT (ASTM D1586) drives the split spoon with a 140 lb hammer falling 30 inches, 18 or 24 inches by sampler length; the blows for the second and third 6 inch intervals sum to N. Penetration under the rods or hammer weight is logged WOR or WOH; over 50 blows within a 6 inch interval ends the test, recorded as 50/x (x = penetration in inches) instead of N. Table 5-2 summarizes the in-situ methods. Two hammer types are in use in the U.S., safety and automatic; the donut hammer was used almost exclusively before about 1970 (Figure 5-3). Energy transfer is typically about 45 % (donut), 60 % (safety) and 80 % (automatic) of the potential energy (Kovacs et al. 1983; Honeycutt et al. 2014) but varies with maintenance, manufacturer, driller and procedure, so yearly calibration to ASTM D4633 is recommended (Figure 5-4). In Finno (1989), borings less than 33 ft apart in uniform sand gave safety hammer N values 1.9 to 2.7 times the automatic hammer values (Figure 5-5), so the hammer type should be recorded on all logs and N reported as N60; Cheney and Chassie (2000) list ten common SPT errors. The manual's design charts and methods use N60 (safety hammer, 60 % energy): Eq. 5-1 corrects for energy, Eq. 5-2 normalizes for overburden with Cn from Eq. 5-3 (Peck et al. 1974, recommended by AASHTO unless the design method says otherwise) or Eq. 5-4 (printed 'Lio and Whitman 1986'). Correlations of N with cohesive soil properties are crude, so correction in cohesive soils is generally not necessary.
key_points: 140 lb hammer, 30 in. drop; N = blows for the 2nd and 3rd 6 in. intervals; 50/x recorded on refusal
Energy transfer typically about 45 % donut, 60 % safety, 80 % automatic; varies by hammer and crew
Calibrate SPT hammers yearly to ASTM D4633
Finno (1989): safety hammer N 1.9 to 2.7 times automatic hammer N in adjacent borings
Record the hammer type on every log; report N60
Design charts in the manual use N60 (60 % energy transfer)
Eq. 5-3: Cn = 0.77 log(40/sigma'vo) <= 2.0, sigma'vo in ksf (Peck et al. 1974, AASHTO)
Eq. 5-4: Cn = (pa/sigma'vo)^n; n = 1 in clays (Olsen 1997), 0.5 in sandy soils
Correction of N values in cohesive soils is generally not necessary
equations: Eq. 5-1: N60 = N (ER / 60); N60 = SPT N corrected for 60 % energy transfer; N = uncorrected field SPT resistance; ER = hammer efficiency from ASTM D4633 energy measurements (p. 108)
Eq. 5-2: (N1)60 = Cn N60; (N1)60 = N corrected for energy and overburden stress; Cn = correction factor (p. 108)
Eq. 5-3: Cn = 0.77 log(40 / sigma'vo) <= 2.0; sigma'vo = vertical effective stress at the sample depth (ksf) (Peck et al. 1974) (p. 108)
Eq. 5-4: Cn = (pa / sigma'vo)^n; pa = atmospheric pressure (ksf); n typically 1 in clays (Olsen 1997) and 0.5 in sandy soils (p. 108)

sections.title: Cone Penetration Test
sections.summary: CPT (ASTM D5778): 1.55 or 2.33 in.2 cone with a 60 degree tip pushed at 0.8 in./sec by a 10 to 40 kip ram; measures qc (qt when corrected for pore pressure), fs and u2; Rf = fs/qt. CPTu, SCPTu and RCPTu variants; Robertson (1990) soil behavior type chart (Figure 5-8). Continuous, repeatable profile with correlations for Dr, phi', su and N60. Soils with N above about 30 to 40 are difficult to penetrate; no samples. 300 to 1200 ft per day.
sections.body: (pp. 109-112) The CPT came to the U.S. in 1965; the electronic cone replaced the mechanical one by the mid 1970s and the piezocone (CPTu) was available in the early 1980s (NCHRP synthesis, Mayne 2007). 300 to 1200 ft can be tested in a day. A 1.55 or 2.33 in.2 cone with a 60 degree tip and a friction sleeve is pushed by a 10 to 40 kip ram at 0.8 in./sec, measuring tip resistance qc, sleeve friction fs and pore pressure u at the u2 position behind the tip; qc corrected for pore pressure is qt and the friction ratio Rf = fs/qt (ASTM D5778; Figures 5-6, 5-7). Modern cones are the piezocone (CPTu, also for dissipation), seismic piezocone (SCPTu, shear wave velocity) and resistivity piezocone (RCPTu); CPT hereafter means with pore pressure. The Robertson (1990) chart (Figure 5-8) gives soil behavior type; correlations give Dr and phi' of cohesionless soils, su of cohesive soils, liquefaction susceptibility and N60, accurate for cohesionless and less so for cohesive soils, and to be confirmed locally. Advantages: a rapid, economical, continuous, operator independent and repeatable profile, used as an equal or superior method at alluvial and liquefiable sites. Limitations: soils with N above about 30 to 40 are hard to penetrate (cones are sometimes pushed through boreholes); marine work needs a fixed platform with casing or submersible equipment; no samples are obtained.
key_points: Cone 1.55 or 2.33 in.2 with a 60 degree tip, pushed at 0.8 in./sec by a 10 to 40 kip ram (ASTM D5778)
Measures qc, fs and u (u2 position); qt = qc corrected for pore pressure; Rf = fs/qt
300 to 1200 ft of sounding per day
CPTu, SCPTu (shear wave velocity) and RCPTu (resistivity) variants
Robertson (1990) soil behavior type chart (Figure 5-8)
Correlations for Dr, phi', su, liquefaction and N60; accurate in cohesionless, less so in cohesive soils
Continuous, economical, operator independent and highly repeatable
Limits: soils with N above about 30 to 40 hard to penetrate; no samples; marine work needs a fixed platform

sections.title: Vane Shear Test
sections.summary: Vane shear test (ASTM D2573) for soft to medium clays: a four bladed vane is rotated in undisturbed soil until it shears, giving peak and remolded strengths and so sensitivity; rod friction is subtracted. Most accurate su for clays with su below 1 ksf. Sensitivity is a qualitative, not quantitative, indicator of setup. Only 13 to 20 ft without casing (Table 5-2).
sections.body: (pp. 112-113) The vane shear test measures the undrained shear strength of soft to medium clays: a four bladed vane is forced into undisturbed soil and rotated until the soil shears (Figure 5-9). Peak and remolded strengths are usually recorded, giving the sensitivity and the resistance to be overcome in driving; friction on the connector rods must be measured and subtracted. It generally gives the most accurate su for clays with su below 1 ksf (ASTM D2573). The sensitivity gives insight into setup potential but is a qualitative, not quantitative, indicator of setup. Table 5-2 adds that it is quick, economical and compares well with unconfined compression at shallow depth, but reaches only 13 to 20 ft without casing.
key_points: For undrained shear strength of soft to medium clays
Four bladed vane forced into undisturbed soil and rotated until the soil shears
Peak and remolded strengths give the sensitivity; rod friction must be subtracted
Most accurate su for clays with su less than 1 ksf (ASTM D2573)
Sensitivity is a qualitative, not quantitative, indicator of soil setup
Only 13 to 20 ft deep without casing the bore hole (Table 5-2)
figures: Figure 5-9: Vane shear test schematic (after Mayne et al. 2001) (p. 113)
sections.applicability: Measurement of undrained shear strength and clay sensitivity for pile design in soft to medium clays.

sections.title: Other In-Situ Tests
sections.summary: Other in-situ tests with limited application to pile design: the dilatometer (5.1.4.1), the pressuremeter (5.1.4.2) and the dynamic cone (5.1.4.3).
sections.body: (p. 113) Other in-situ tests with limited application to pile foundation design are the dilatometer (Section 5.1.4.1), the pressuremeter (5.1.4.2) and the dynamic cone (5.1.4.3).
key_points: Dilatometer, pressuremeter and dynamic cone have limited application to pile design
sections.applicability: Secondary in-situ testing devices with limited direct application to driven pile design.

sections.title: Dilatometer Test
sections.body: (p. 114) The DMT was developed in Italy in the early 1970s and introduced in the U.S. in 1979. It is generally pushed hydraulically (it may be driven); at 8 inch test increments 100 to 300 ft can be sounded a day. Its main use in pile design is delineating stratigraphy and interpreted soil properties, a task the CPT/CPTu generally suits better. It may be useful for laterally loaded piles; for axially loaded piles it has limited direct value (ASTM D6635).
key_points: Developed in Italy, early 1970s; in the U.S. since 1979; pushed hydraulically or driven
100 to 300 ft per day at 8 in. test increments
CPT/CPTu generally better suited to stratigraphy; DMT potentially useful for laterally loaded piles
Limited direct value for axially loaded piles (ASTM D6635)
sections.applicability: Dilatometer testing in pile design (stratigraphy, laterally loaded piles).

sections.title: Pressuremeter Tests
sections.body: (p. 114) The PMT imparts lateral pressure to soil or rock and gives shear strength and compressibility from the pressure-volume curve, in soft or fissured clays, sands, gravels and soft rock. It yields the elastic modulus, at-rest horizontal earth pressure, creep pressure and limit pressure. It is a useful design tool for laterally loaded piles, including p-y curves, but of limited value for vertically loaded piles. Pile design with PMT data: FHWA-IP-89-008 (Briaud 1989); procedure ASTM D4719.
key_points: Lateral pressure test giving modulus, at-rest horizontal pressure, creep pressure and limit pressure
Soft and fissured clays, sands, gravels and soft rock can be tested
Useful for laterally loaded piles and p-y curves; limited value for vertically loaded piles
Design procedures: FHWA-IP-89-008 (Briaud 1989); test: ASTM D4719
sections.applicability: Pressuremeter testing for laterally loaded pile design.

sections.title: Dynamic Cone
sections.body: (pp. 114-115) Two dynamic penetrometers with conical points exist. The common type has a shaft smaller than the cone, so in theory it measures only point resistance; the other has shaft and cone of the same diameter and records skin friction and point resistance together, inseparably. Equations exist for pile resistance from dynamic cone data, but they are not used extensively and the dynamic cone is not recommended for final foundation design unless local correlations with load tests to geotechnical failure exist. Table 5-2: qualitative density and stratigraphy, best in sand and gravel, not in clay, useful where the static cone refuses.
key_points: Common type: shaft smaller than the cone, measuring point resistance only in theory
Equal diameter type records skin friction and point resistance together, not separable
Not recommended for final design without local correlations with load tests to geotechnical failure
Qualitative density and stratigraphy; best in sand and gravel, not suitable in clay (Table 5-2)
sections.applicability: Dynamic cone penetrometer use in pile design (qualitative only).

sections.title: Soil Parameters
sections.summary: Overview of geomaterial parameters for pile design. Index properties segregate soil strata; engineering properties (shear strength, compressibility, permeability) drive design decisions. Shear strength governs strength limit states; compressibility governs service limit states; permeability informs drivability and constructability.
sections.body: (p. 115) Index and engineering properties come from field and laboratory testing. Index tests separate soil and rock types into design strata and help with constructability and preliminary pile selection. Engineering properties are shear strength, compressibility and permeability: shear strength gives the geotechnical resistances and compressibility the service limit state checks; permeability is not generally quantified, but slow draining soils can affect drivability. See Bowles (1992), GEC-5 (Sabatini et al. 2002) and Samtani and Nowatzki (2006).
key_points: Index properties segregate soil and rock types for subsurface strata division
Engineering properties: shear strength, compressibility, permeability
Shear strength determines driven pile geotechnical resistances (strength limit state)
Compressibility checks serviceability limit states
Permeability not quantified for pile design but influences drivability
Further information in Bowles (1992), GEC-5 (Sabatini et al. 2002), and Samtani and Nowatzki (2006)
sections.applicability: Overview of soil parameters needed for driven pile foundation design.

sections.title: Soil Classification and Index Properties
sections.summary: USCS (ASTM D2487) is used for deep foundation design. Index tests (Table 5-3): particle size (D422), Atterberg limits (D4318), moisture (D2216), specific gravity, unit weight. Sensitivity St = qu undisturbed/qu remolded (Eq. 5-5); Table 5-4: NC clays 2-8, marine clays 10-80, OC clays 1-4, fissured clays 0.5-2. Remolded strength during driving about 1/3 to 1/2 of undisturbed.
sections.body: (pp. 115-118) AASHTO classification is used for pavements and the USCS for nearly all other geotechnical work; the USCS is better suited to deep foundations and is used solely in the manual. Routine index tests are particle size distribution, Atterberg limits and moisture content, with specific gravity and unit weight (Table 5-3, modified from Brown et al. 2010). Fines content and gradation of cohesionless soils and remolded strength of cohesive soils matter for drivability and setup: high fines lower the friction angle at similar density, affect drainage and pore pressure in driving, and make setup more likely; gradation also bears on densification and liquefaction. Cohesive soils can lose much of their strength when remolded in driving, and estimating the strength at driving and the setup gain is key to economical design (Chapter 7). Sensitivity (Eq. 5-5) is a qualitative indication of setup, best measured in-situ with the vane. Table 5-4 (Sowers 1979) gives typical sensitivities; Terzaghi and Peck (1967) noted that clays with sensitivity below 16 generally regain part or all of their strength with time, and the remolded strength during driving is expected to be about 1/3 to 1/2 of the undisturbed strength.
key_points: USCS (ASTM D2487) is used solely in the manual; AASHTO classification is for pavements
Index tests: particle size, Atterberg limits, moisture content, specific gravity, unit weight (Table 5-3)
High fines lower phi' at similar density, affect drainage during driving and make setup more likely
Eq. 5-5: St = qu undisturbed / qu remolded; best measured in-situ with the vane
Table 5-4: NC medium plasticity clay 2-8; marine clays 10-80; OC clays 1-4; fissured clays 0.5-2
Clays with sensitivity below 16 generally regain part or all of their strength with time (Terzaghi and Peck 1967)
Remolded strength during driving about 1/3 to 1/2 of the undisturbed strength
equations: Eq. 5-5: St = qu (undisturbed) / qu (remolded); St = sensitivity of a cohesive soil (p. 117)
tables: Table 5-3: Soil Index Tests used for Driven Pile Design (modified from Brown et al. 2010) (p. 116)
Table 5-4: Typical Values of Sensitivity (after Sowers 1979) (p. 117)
sections.applicability: Soil classification, index testing, and sensitivity evaluation for driven pile design and drivability assessment.

sections.title: In-Situ Stress
sections.summary: sigma' = sigma - u (Eq. 5-6); sigma = sum gamma_i h_i (Eq. 5-7); u = gamma_w h_w (Eq. 5-8); sigma'vo = sum gamma_i h_i - gamma_w h_w (Eq. 5-9); sigma'ho = Ko sigma'vo (Eq. 5-10). Use accurate unit weights in the partially saturated vadose zone. Effective stress analysis for free draining clean sands; for clays and slow draining soils, where pore pressure rises on loading, a total stress analysis may be practical.
sections.body: (pp. 118-119) The in-situ stress at depth is needed for geotechnical resistance (detail in Sabatini et al. 2002, Samtani and Nowatzki 2006, Das 2007). Effective stress is total stress less pore pressure (Eq. 5-6); total stress sums unit weight times thickness over the strata (Eq. 5-7); pore pressure is the unit weight of water times the pressure head (Eq. 5-8); hence the vertical effective stress (Eq. 5-9). Above the water table coarse soils may be assumed dry but are more likely partially saturated with capillary suction in the vadose zone, so accurate unit weights should be used. Lateral resistance depends on the horizontal effective stress from Ko (Eq. 5-10). Effective stress parameters suit piles in free draining clean sands, where pore pressure dissipates almost immediately; total stress may be practical in clays and slow draining soils.
key_points: Eq. 5-6: sigma' = sigma - u
Eq. 5-7: sigma = sum(gamma_i h_i); Eq. 5-8: u = gamma_w h_w
Eq. 5-9: sigma'vo = sum(gamma_i h_i) - gamma_w h_w
Eq. 5-10: sigma'ho = Ko sigma'vo
Use accurate unit weights in the partially saturated vadose zone
Effective stress analysis for free draining clean sands; total stress may be practical for slow draining clays
equations: Eq. 5-6: sigma' = sigma - u; sigma' = effective stress; sigma = total stress; u = pore water pressure (p. 118)
Eq. 5-7: sigma = sum over i = 1 to n of (gamma_i h_i); gamma_i = total unit weight and h_i = thickness of stratum i (p. 118)
Eq. 5-8: u = gamma_w h_w; gamma_w = unit weight of water; h_w = pressure head (p. 118)
Eq. 5-9: sigma'vo = sum over i = 1 to n of (gamma_i h_i) - gamma_w h_w; vertical effective stress at depth (p. 118)
Eq. 5-10: sigma'ho = Ko sigma'vo; Ko = at rest lateral earth pressure coefficient (p. 119)
sections.applicability: Calculation of in-situ stress state for driven pile geotechnical resistance calculations.

sections.title: Shear Strength
sections.summary: Mohr-Coulomb: tau = c + sigma tan phi total stress (Eq. 5-11); tau = c' + sigma' tan phi' effective stress (Eq. 5-12, c' usually zero); tau = c = su undrained (phi = 0, Eq. 5-13). Setup: strength gain in saturated NC to moderately OC clays; relaxation: loss in heavily OC clays, dense silts, dense fine sands, weak laminated rock.
sections.body: (pp. 119-121) Shear strength is the internal resistance per unit area on a plane, set by compositional, environmental and in-situ factors and by the manner (static, dynamic, cyclic) and rate of loading. GEC-5 notes strength can change between driving and loading: setup (gain) in saturated NC to moderately OC clays and fine-grained material, relaxation (loss) in heavily OC clays, dense silts, dense fine sands and weak laminated rock; dewatering, surface loading and excavation change the effective stress, and granular soils may densify from driving. The Mohr-Coulomb criterion is the only model discussed: Eq. 5-11 (total stress, undrained phi and c) and Eq. 5-12 (effective stress); c' is usually taken as zero in drained cohesionless soils but may be included with care for cemented, partially saturated or heavily OC soils, given its strong influence. For short-term undrained loading of cohesive soils phi = 0 and Eq. 5-13 applies. Rapid loading of slow draining soils generates excess pore pressure not easily quantified, and the tested cohesion may be taken as the design shear strength.
key_points: Setup: strength gain with time in saturated NC to moderately OC clays and fine-grained material
Relaxation: strength loss in heavily OC clays, dense silts, dense fine sands and weak laminated rock
Dewatering, surface loading and excavation can change strength; granular soils may densify from driving
Eq. 5-11: tau = c + sigma tan phi (total stress)
Eq. 5-12: tau = c' + sigma' tan phi' (effective stress); c' usually zero, include only with care
Eq. 5-13: tau = c = su for short-term undrained loading of cohesive soils (phi = 0)
equations: Eq. 5-11: tau = c + sigma tan phi; tau = shear strength; c = cohesion; sigma = total normal stress on the failure plane; phi = angle of internal friction (p. 120)
Eq. 5-12: tau = c' + sigma' tan phi'; c' = effective cohesion; sigma' = effective normal stress on the failure plane; phi' = effective stress friction angle (p. 120)
Eq. 5-13: tau = c = su; su = undrained shear strength (p. 120)
sections.applicability: Shear strength determination for driven pile geotechnical resistance calculations under drained and undrained conditions.

sections.title: Laboratory Tests for Soil Shear Strength
sections.body: (p. 121) Three laboratory methods are commonly used for shear strength: the direct shear test (AASHTO T236 / ASTM D3080), the unconfined compression test (AASHTO T208 / ASTM D2166) and the triaxial compression test (AASHTO T234 / ASTM D2850); details in GEC-5 and the ASTM standards.
key_points: Direct shear (AASHTO T236 / ASTM D3080)
Unconfined compression (AASHTO T208 / ASTM D2166)
Triaxial compression (AASHTO T234 / ASTM D2850)
sections.applicability: Selecting laboratory shear strength tests for pile design.

sections.title: Direct Shear
sections.body: (p. 121) A soil sample in a box split at mid height is loaded normally and one half is pushed past the other; shear stress (horizontal force over area) is plotted against horizontal deformation, and at least three normal stresses give c and phi. Bowles (1977): plane strain direct shear phi is about 1.1 times triaxial phi. Direct shear is mostly run on recompacted granular soils, which may not represent the field, and is generally not recommended for cohesive soils because drainage cannot be controlled.
key_points: At least three normal stresses give c and phi
phi from plane strain direct shear is about 1.1 times triaxial phi (Bowles 1977)
Mostly on recompacted granular soils; not recommended for cohesive soils (no drainage control)
sections.applicability: Direct shear testing for granular soil strength.

sections.title: Unconfined Compression
sections.body: (pp. 121-122) An axial load is applied to a cylindrical sample at zero confining pressure until failure, and the shear strength is half the axial stress at failure. It is run only on cohesive soil and rock. Samples from depth or with sand seams, fissures or slickensides can give misleadingly low strengths because the confining stress is removed; triaxial tests are better in those cases.
key_points: Shear strength = one half the axial stress at failure, zero confining pressure
Only for cohesive soil and rock samples
Deep or fissured, slickensided, sand-seamed samples can give misleadingly low strengths; use triaxial tests
sections.applicability: Unconfined compression testing of cohesive soil and rock.

sections.title: Triaxial Compression Test
sections.body: (p. 122) The most versatile strength test: a membrane-encased cylinder under confining pressure is sheared axially with drainage controlled at its ends, giving c and phi, and c' and phi' when drained or with pore pressure measurement. Drainage, consolidation and loading are chosen to model the field. Types: unconsolidated undrained (UU, ASTM D2850), consolidated undrained (CU, ASTM D4767) and consolidated drained (CD, ASTM D7181). UU tests are more reliable than unconfined compression; CU tests with pore pressure give both effective and total stress parameters.
key_points: Most versatile laboratory shear strength test
UU (ASTM D2850), CU (ASTM D4767), CD (ASTM D7181)
UU more reliable than unconfined compression
CU with pore pressure measurement gives effective and total stress parameters
sections.applicability: Triaxial testing for total and effective stress parameters.

sections.title: Effective Stress Friction Angle Correlations, Cohesionless Soils
sections.summary: SPT: AASHTO Table 5-5 ((N1)60 < 4: 25-30 deg to 50: 38-43 deg), Meyerhof Table 5-6 (-5 deg clayey sand, +5 deg gravelly sand), Schmertmann Eq. 5-14 phi' = arctan{[N60/(12.2 + 20.3 sigma'vo/pa)]^0.34}, Hatanaka and Uchida Eq. 5-15 phi' = sqrt(20(N1)60) + 20, Kulhawy and Chen Eq. 5-16 phi' = 27.5 + 9.2 log(N1)60. CPT: Meyerhof Table 5-7, Robertson and Campanella Eq. 5-17 phi' = arctan[0.1 + 0.38 log(qc/sigma'vo)]. Rockfill: Figure 5-10 with Table 5-8 grades.
sections.body: (pp. 122-127) phi' in cohesionless soil is usually correlated from SPT N or CPT qc; the designer should know whether a correlation uses uncorrected N or (N1)60 (AASHTO 2014). The AASHTO (N1)60 correlation (Table 5-5, modified after Bowles 1997) is the basis of the AASHTO resistance factor calibrations. GEC-5 gives Meyerhof's (1956) correlation for relatively clean sands (Table 5-6), with phi' reduced 5 degrees for clayey sand and increased 5 degrees for gravelly sand; in saturated fine or silty sand N = 15 + (N' - 15)/2 for N' > 15. Schmertmann (1975), for clean sands below 7 ft, is approximated by Kulhawy and Mayne (1990) as Eq. 5-14; Hatanaka and Uchida (1996), from frozen samples of fine and medium sand, give Eq. 5-15; Kulhawy and Chen (2007), 57 sand and gravel samples (r2 = 0.356), give Eq. 5-16. For the CPT, Meyerhof (1976) is Table 5-7 and Robertson and Campanella (1983) on clean quartz sand, as presented by Kulhawy and Mayne (1990), is Eq. 5-17. Where cobbles and boulders inflate N, phi' of rockfills, gravels and sands comes from Figure 5-10 with the rockfill grade from particle strength (Table 5-8) and the average effective normal stress, as a secant angle (Terzaghi et al. 1996). Table 5-8's caption refers to 'Figure 5-12' while the text uses Figure 5-10.
key_points: Know whether a correlation uses N or (N1)60 (AASHTO 2014)
Table 5-6 (Meyerhof 1956): very loose N < 4, phi' < 30 to very dense N > 50, phi' > 45; -5 deg clayey sand, +5 deg gravelly sand
Saturated fine or silty sand: N = 15 + (N' - 15)/2 for N' > 15
Eq. 5-14 (Schmertmann 1975 via Kulhawy and Mayne 1990): phi' = arctan{[N60 / (12.2 + 20.3 sigma'vo/pa)]^0.34}
Eq. 5-15 (Hatanaka and Uchida 1996): phi' = sqrt(20 (N1)60) + 20
Eq. 5-16 (Kulhawy and Chen 2007): phi' = 27.5 + 9.2 log[(N1)60]
Table 5-7 (Meyerhof 1976): qc < 4 tsf, phi' < 30 to qc > 50 tsf, phi' > 45

sections.title: Fully Drained Shear Strength of Fine-Grained Cohesive Soils
sections.summary: Effective stress parameters phi' and c' from CD triaxial, CD direct shear, or CU triaxial with pore pressure measurements. Applicable for long-term pile resistance after pore pressures dissipate. Preliminary phi' from plasticity index using Terzaghi et al. (1996) correlation (Fig 5-11). Use c' = 0 for preliminary estimates from PI correlation (GEC-5).
sections.body: (p. 127) Effective stress analysis can be used for fine-grained soils under fully drained loading, to assess pile resistance long after installation when pore pressures have stabilized. AASHTO (2014) recommends laboratory tests for phi' and c': consolidated drained direct shear, CD triaxial, or CU triaxial with pore pressure measurement, with attention to shear rate and to full dissipation (drained) or equalization (undrained) of pore pressure. Preliminary phi' may come from the plasticity index by the Terzaghi et al. (1996) correlation for clays and shale (Figure 5-11), with c' = 0 per GEC-5.
key_points: Effective stress analysis for fine-grained soils under fully drained loading
Useful for assessing pile resistances long after installation when pore pressures have stabilized
AASHTO recommends laboratory testing (CD, CU with pore pressure) for phi' and c'
Preliminary phi' estimates from plasticity index using Terzaghi et al. (1996) correlation
GEC-5 recommends c' = 0 for preliminary estimates from PI correlation
Consideration for shear rate and complete dissipation of excess pore pressure in lab testing
figures: Figure 5-11: Relationship between phi' and PI (after Terzaghi et al. 1996) (p. 127)
sections.applicability: Effective stress shear strength parameters for fine-grained cohesive soils in long-term pile resistance evaluations.

sections.title: Undrained Shear Strength of Fine-Grained Cohesive Soils
sections.summary: su from UC/UU/CU tests (AASHTO prefers CU and UU) or correlations: CPT su = (qc - sigma'vo)/Nk, Nk 14-16 (Eq. 5-18); SPT su = f1 N60 pa/100, f1 = 4.5 (PI 50) to 5.5 (PI 15) (Eq. 5-19); vane su = 6Tv/[7 pi dv^3] for hv/dv = 2 (Eq. 5-20) with Bjerrum mu = 2.5 PI^-0.3 <= 1.1 (Eq. 5-21). su = qu/2; Table 5-9 (N to qu) is crude, preliminary only.
sections.body: (pp. 127-129) su may be measured in the laboratory (recommended, on undisturbed samples: UC, UU or CU; AASHTO recommends CU and UU where possible, CU reconsolidating to in-situ stress) or correlated with in-situ tests where good samples cannot be had. Disturbance, strain rate and drainage affect results, generally conservatively (Brown et al. 2010). CPT: Eq. 5-18 with Nk typically 14 to 16 (about 10 to 18), calibrated locally. SPT: Eq. 5-19 (Stroud 1974, 1989) with f1 = 4.5 at PI = 50 and 5.5 at PI = 15. Table 5-9 (Bowles 1977) relates uncorrected N to qu and saturated unit weight, with su = qu/2; N to su correlations are crude, for preliminary estimates only. Vane: Eq. 5-20 for hv/dv = 2 (GEC-5) and Bjerrum's (1972) correction Eq. 5-21; peak and residual strengths give the sensitivity (Eq. 5-5).
key_points: Laboratory testing of undisturbed samples recommended; AASHTO recommends CU and UU where possible
Eq. 5-18: su = (qc - sigma'vo)/Nk, Nk typically 14 to 16 (about 10 to 18); calibrate locally
Table 5-9: very soft qu 0-0.5 ksf, N 0-2 up to hard qu 8.0+ ksf, N 32+
su = qu/2; N to su correlations are crude, for preliminary estimates only
Eq. 5-20: su = 6 Tv / [7 pi (dv)^3] for hv/dv = 2

sections.title: Deformation
sections.summary: Deformation is the soil response to load and governs the serviceability limit state: elastic modulus (Section 5.2.4.1, Eqs. 5-22, 5-23, Tables 5-10 to 5-12) and primary consolidation settlement (Section 5.2.4.2, Eqs. 5-24 to 5-26).
sections.body: (p. 130) Deformation is the soil response to load; tolerable deformations relate to the serviceability limit state, and the needed modulus and consolidation parameters come from tests that quantify strain. Elastic deformation is Section 5.2.4.1 and primary consolidation 5.2.4.2.
key_points: Tolerable deformations relate to the serviceability limit state
Elastic modulus (5.2.4.1) and consolidation parameters (5.2.4.2) come from tests that measure strain
sections.applicability: Elastic modulus estimation and consolidation settlement calculations for driven pile serviceability limit state.

sections.title: Elastic Deformation
sections.body: (pp. 130-132) The modulus E comes from strain under load by Hooke's law (Eq. 5-22) or from correlations. The 50 % secant modulus E50 runs from the origin to half the peak stress (Figure 5-12). The shear modulus follows from E and Poisson ratio (Eq. 5-23); elastic deformation is treated further in Chapter 7. Values compiled by Bowles (1988) and the Navy (1982) and tabulated by AASHTO (2014) give preliminary estimates, with SPT and CPT correlations (Tables 5-10 to 5-12, modified from AASHTO); testing should confirm or supersede them.
key_points: Eq. 5-22: sigma = E epsilon (Hooke's law)
E50: secant from the origin to half the peak stress (Figure 5-12)
Table 5-10: soft sensitive clay 50-300 ksf; dense sand 1,000-1,600 ksf; dense gravel 2,000-4,000 ksf
Table 5-11: Es = 8 (N1)60 silts, 14 (N1)60 clean fine-medium sands, 20 (N1)60 coarse sands, 24 (N1)60 gravels (ksf)
Table 5-12: Es = 2 qc for sandy soils
Tabulated values are preliminary; testing should confirm or supersede them
equations: Eq. 5-22: sigma = E epsilon; sigma = stress; E = elastic modulus; epsilon = strain (p. 130)
Eq. 5-23: G = E / [2 (1 + v)]; G = shear modulus; v = Poisson ratio (p. 130)
figures: Figure 5-12: Soil stress strain curve and 50% secant modulus (after Brown et al. 2010) (p. 131)
tables: Table 5-10: Estimating Soil Modulus, Es, Based on Soil Type (after AASHTO 2014) (p. 131)
Table 5-11: Estimating Soil Modulus, Es, from SPT N value (after AASHTO 2014) (p. 132)
Table 5-12: Estimating Soil Modulus, Es, from Cone Resistance, qc (after AASHTO 2014) (p. 132)
sections.applicability: Elastic soil modulus estimates for pile deformation analysis.

sections.title: Primary Consolidation Settlement
sections.body: (pp. 132-134) The one dimensional consolidation test (AASHTO T216 / ASTM D2435) gives the coefficient of consolidation cv, compression index Cc, recompression or swell index Cr (Cs) and secondary compression index C_alpha; void ratio against log effective stress gives the preconsolidation stress sigma_p (Figure 5-13), and log time against compression gives cv. Primary consolidation settlement of a cohesive layer follows Eq. 5-24 (normally consolidated, sigma'vo = sigma_p), Eq. 5-25 (overconsolidated, sigma'vo + delta_sigma <= sigma_p) and Eq. 5-26 (overconsolidated, sigma'vo + delta_sigma > sigma_p).
key_points: Consolidation test (AASHTO T216 / ASTM D2435) gives cv, Cc, Cr (Cs) and C_alpha
e-log sigma'v curve gives the preconsolidation stress sigma_p (Figure 5-13)
Eq. 5-24 NC: Sc = sum Cc/(1+eo) Ho log[(sigma'vo + delta_sigma)/sigma'vo]
Eq. 5-25 OC, within recompression: same with Cr
Eq. 5-26 OC, beyond sigma_p: Cr term to sigma_p plus Cc term beyond
equations: Eq. 5-24: Sc = sum over i to n of [Cc / (1 + eo)] Ho log[(sigma'vo + delta_sigma) / sigma'vo], for normally consolidated layers (sigma'vo = sigma_p) (p. 133)
Eq. 5-25: Sc = sum over i to n of [Cr / (1 + eo)] Ho log[(sigma'vo + delta_sigma) / sigma'vo], for overconsolidated soil with sigma'vo + delta_sigma <= sigma_p (p. 133)

Eq. 5-26: Sc = sum over i to n of {[Cr / (1 + eo)] Ho log(sigma_p / sigma'vo) + [Cc / (1 + eo)] Ho log[(sigma'vo + delta_sigma) / sigma_p]}, for sigma'vo + delta_sigma > sigma_p; Sc = primary consolidation settlement; eo = initial void ratio; Ho = initial layer thickness; sigma_p = preconsolidation stress; sigma'vo = average vertical effective stress at the layer mid-point before loading; delta_sigma = added stress at the mid-point (p. 134)
figures: Figure 5-13: Plot of Void Ratio vs Vertical Effective Stress from consolidation test (p. 133)
sections.applicability: Primary consolidation settlement of cohesive layers below pile groups.

sections.title: Electro Chemical Properties
sections.summary: Electro chemical tests assess how aggressive soil and groundwater are to pile materials: pH (AASHTO T289/ASTM D4972), resistivity (T288/D1125), sulfate ion (T290/D4230), chloride ion (T291/D512). Steel corrosion or concrete disintegration rates may be needed for long-term structural resistance. The text refers to Section 6.14 for environmental effects on pile selection; the aggressive-environment guidance is Section 6.12.
sections.body: (p. 134) Soil and groundwater can hold constituents harmful to pile materials; electro chemical tests show how aggressive the conditions are and the potential for deterioration, and corrosion rates for steel or disintegration rates for concrete may be needed to judge long-term structural resistance. Tests: pH (AASHTO T289 / ASTM D4972), resistivity (AASHTO T288 / ASTM D1125), sulfate ion content (AASHTO T290 / ASTM D4230) and chloride ion content (AASHTO T291 / ASTM D512). The text refers to Section 6.14 of Chapter 6 for environmental effects on section selection; the aggressive-environment guidance is printed in Section 6.12.
key_points: Electro chemical tests assess aggressiveness of subsurface conditions for pile materials
Tests: pH, resistivity, sulfate ion content, chloride ion content
Corrosion rates for steel piles and disintegration rates for concrete may be required
Results used for long-term structural resistance evaluation and pile section selection
sections.applicability: Assessment of subsurface chemical conditions for pile material durability and structural resistance.

sections.title: Rock Parameters
sections.summary: Rock properties govern end bearing and long-term deformation; shallow rock may need predrilling for minimum penetration. Intact rock (cores) is distinguished from the rock mass with its discontinuities. Index properties and classification 5.3.1, shear strength 5.3.2, deformation 5.3.3; soft and hard rock for driving are defined in 5.5.2.
sections.body: (pp. 134-135) Rock properties are needed for end bearing and long-term deformation; shallow rock may need predrilling to meet minimum penetration. Intact rock (consolidated, cemented particles tested on cores) is distinguished from the rock mass, which joints, faults and bedding break up (Brown et al. 2010).
key_points: Rock properties needed for end bearing and long-term deformation
Shallow rock may need predrilling to satisfy minimum penetration
Intact rock (tested on cores) versus rock mass (with joints, faults, bedding)
sections.applicability: Rock classification, strength, and deformation parameters for driven piles bearing on or driven to rock.

sections.title: Rock Index Properties and Classification
sections.body: (p. 135) Rock classification should record color, texture, lithology (igneous, metamorphic, sedimentary), field hardness, weathering and discontinuities. The slake durability test (ASTM D4644) shows whether weak rocks such as shale, mudstone and siltstone will weather and deteriorate, as they may fracture in driving; low indices may flag deposits where piles relax. Dried fragments are rotated in a wire mesh drum in water for 10 minutes, dried, and the cycle repeated; the final over initial dry weight is the index ID, and ID below 60 % means a rock prone to rapid degradation.
key_points: Classify by color, texture, lithology, field hardness, weathering and discontinuities
Slake durability (ASTM D4644) for shale, mudstone, siltstone; two 10 minute cycles
ID below 60 % indicates rock prone to rapid degradation; low ID may flag pile relaxation
sections.applicability: Rock classification and slake durability for driven piles in weak rock.

sections.title: Rock Mass Shear Strength
sections.body: (p. 135) Rock strength is usually measured by uniaxial compression of prepared cores (ASTM D7012): axial strain gives the elastic modulus and the peak load over area gives the unconfined compressive strength qu, which AASHTO and other methods use for the nominal resistance of end bearing piles on rock.
key_points: Uniaxial compression of cores (ASTM D7012) gives qu and the elastic modulus
qu is used by AASHTO and other methods for end bearing piles on rock
sections.applicability: Rock strength for end bearing piles on rock.

sections.title: Rock Mass Deformation
sections.body: (p. 136) Rock deformation is typically elastic and is generally not a design consideration, as piles penetrate weak rock or stop on hard rock; for heavily loaded piles just into or above soil-like weak rock such as marl, rock mass deformation properties may be needed, estimated from correlations of RQD, GSI and core recovery with rock mass modulus. Uniaxial tests give E (E50 at half the peak deviator stress) and, with diametral measurement, Poisson ratio; Kulhawy's (1978) tables, reproduced in Samtani and Nowatzki (2006) and AASHTO (2014) Table C10.4.6.5-1, estimate them.
key_points: Rock deformation is generally not a design consideration for driven piles
Needed for heavily loaded piles in or above soil-like weak rock (e.g., marl)
Rock mass modulus from correlations with RQD, GSI and core recovery
Kulhawy (1978) tables of E and Poisson ratio (AASHTO Table C10.4.6.5-1)
sections.applicability: Rock mass modulus for piles bearing in weak rock.

sections.title: Considerations for Pile Drivability
sections.summary: AASHTO Article 10.7.8 calls for a drivability evaluation in design. Boulders, artesian conditions, fines content, angularity, density and plasticity affect drivability. Large quakes and high rebound occur in dense silty sand, hard silty clay, glacial tills and other saturated fine soils (pore pressure near the toe; Cosentino et al. 2010). Use a range of dynamic soil properties (some sands, CH and MH soils). Weathered shale and siltstone may lose end bearing with time or shatter when adjacent piles are driven.
sections.body: (pp. 136-137) AASHTO Article 10.7.8 calls for a drivability evaluation during design. Drivability is the ability to drive the pile to the estimated nominal axial resistance anticipated during driving at or above the required penetration depth, within the driving stress limits of the pile material; it needs a detailed identification of the subsurface and its response to installation. Obvious issues are boulders above the bearing strata (pile damage) and artesian conditions (reduced resistance); fines content, angularity, density and high plasticity also matter. Large soil quakes or high elastic behavior have been reported in dense silty sand, hard silty clay, glacial tills and other fine grained saturated soils (Likins 1983; Hannigan 1985; Hussein et al. 2006). In Florida DOT research (Cosentino et al. 2010) high rebound came from pore pressure rising near the toe during driving, leading to refusal, and lessened when driving paused; in the Hawthorn Group formation high silt content and changes in N within strata correlated with high rebound zones. Thompson and Goble (1988) summarized nine projects in sand with high dynamic resistance and no clear depositional, geologic or mineralogical relationship, so drivability analyses should consider a range of dynamic soil properties, as also in highly plastic CH and MH soils where conventional values may underestimate the dynamic resistance. In weathered shale and siltstone, end bearing can drop with time as locked-in horizontal stresses release, and driving adjacent piles to or below the same depth can shatter weak rock; local experience and methods help.
key_points: AASHTO Article 10.7.8 requires drivability evaluation during design stage
Drivability: ability to drive pile to required resistance and penetration within material stress limits
Boulders, artesian conditions, fine content, angularity, density, and plasticity all influence drivability
High elastic rebound (soil quakes) reported in dense silty sand, hard silty clay, glacial tills
High silt content and N value changes within strata correlate with high elastic rebound
Range of dynamic soil properties should be evaluated in drivability analyses
Highly plastic CH and MH soils may produce dynamic resistances exceeding conventional values
Weathered rock (shale, siltstone) may exhibit reduction in end bearing resistance over time
Driving adjacent piles can shatter weak rock and reduce end bearing
sections.applicability: Identification of subsurface conditions that influence pile drivability analysis and construction planning.

sections.title: Selection of Parameters for Design and Construction
sections.summary: Parameters come from site specific tests and must match the design method, since some resistance factors rest on a specific N-phi or N-su correlation or phi limit. Soil parameters 5.5.1 (phi' at most 32 deg soft rounded and 36 deg hard angular gravel for shaft resistance), rock 5.5.2 (soft rock penetrable by driving, hard rock not), site variability 5.5.3 (COV low < 25 %, medium 25-40 %, high >= 40 %; Table 5-14).
sections.body: (pp. 137-138) Soil and rock parameters should be selected from site specific in-situ and laboratory results and the relevant design methods. Some resistance factors were developed for a specific method based on a specific N to phi or N to su correlation or a limit on the maximum friction angle. Soil parameters are Section 5.5.1, rock parameters 5.5.2 and site variability 5.5.3.
key_points: Select parameters from site specific test results and the relevant design method
Some resistance factors rest on a specific N-phi or N-su correlation or a phi limit
sections.applicability: Selection of geomaterial design parameters with appropriate consideration of site variability and design method requirements.

sections.title: Soil Parameters
sections.body: (p. 138) Preliminary strength and density estimates often come from SPT correlations (the text cites Sections 5.2.3.3 and 5.2.3.4) and should be confirmed by further in-situ and laboratory tests, with each layer's variability, strength, compressibility and index properties quantified. In coarse granular deposits phi' should be chosen conservatively: static analyses often overpredict shaft resistance, particularly in uniform or rounded deposits. Cheney and Chassie (1993) neglected particle interlock, giving a maximum phi' for shaft resistance of 32 degrees in soft rounded gravel and 36 degrees in hard angular gravel; toe resistance uses phi' by normal procedures. AASHTO Article 10.4 resistance factors were developed for specific methods and procedures, so parameters should be obtained in the prescribed manner (Chapter 7).
key_points: SPT correlations for preliminary estimates; confirm with in-situ and laboratory tests
Select phi' conservatively in coarse granular deposits; static analyses often overpredict shaft resistance
Shaft resistance in gravel: phi' at most 32 deg soft rounded, 36 deg hard angular (Cheney and Chassie 1993)
Toe resistance phi' by normal procedures
AASHTO Article 10.4 resistance factors assume parameters obtained in the prescribed manner
sections.applicability: Selecting soil design parameters consistent with the static analysis method.

sections.title: Rock Parameters
sections.body: (pp. 138-140) Parameters are needed for piles driven into soft rock or to hard rock; cores of both should be taken with weathering and fracturing, and local experience is invaluable. No clear definition exists: in many intact rock systems hard soil grades to soft rock at qu of about 20 ksf and soft to hard rock between 200 and 1000 ksf. For driven piles soft rock is rock that driving can penetrate and hard rock is rock it cannot, so piles are driven into soft rock and to hard rock. Soft rocks are hard to sample and test (too strong for soil equipment, too weak for rock equipment) and may crumble, laminate, disaggregate, slake or vary with weathering; Kanji (2014) lists usual types (Table 5-13). For soft and weak rock, quantify classification, recovery, RQD, qu, density and slake durability; for hard rock, where toe damage or yielding precedes rock failure, the same except slake durability.
key_points: Hard soil to soft rock at qu of about 20 ksf; soft to hard rock between 200 and 1000 ksf
Soft rock: penetrable by pile driving; hard rock: not penetrable; piles are driven into soft rock and to hard rock
Soft rocks are difficult to sample and test; may crumble, slake or vary with weathering
Table 5-13: soft rock types by sedimentary, igneous and metamorphic class (Kanji 2014)
Soft rock: quantify classification, recovery, RQD, qu, density and slake durability
Hard rock: toe damage or yielding occurs before rock failure; quantify classification, recovery, RQD, qu, density
tables: Table 5-13: Usual Types of Soft Rocks (after Kanji 2014) (p. 139)
sections.applicability: Rock design parameters for piles driven into soft rock or to hard rock.

sections.title: Site Variability
sections.body: (pp. 140-141) Test results within a seemingly uniform profile often conflict, and parameter selection then rests on judgment (GEC-5 Chapter 8): find inconsistent results or use historical information. Site variability is within the site, not between sites, and is judged for each substructure from the nearest borings or tests. Paikowsky et al. (2004): (1) average the strength parameters of each significant bearing layer at each boring, (2) check the COV of those averages between borings, (3) categorize: COV < 25 % low, 25 % <= COV < 40 % medium, COV >= 40 % high. A high COV calls for more or different tests, judgment or smaller sub-sites. Table 5-14 (Duncan and Wright 2005) gives COVs from many sources, not for specific cases; GEC-5 suggests statistics and sensitivity analyses as a minimum, COV being the standard deviation over the mean.
key_points: Site variability is within a site, judged for each substructure location
Paikowsky et al. (2004): average layer parameters per boring, check COV between borings, categorize
COV < 25 % low; 25 % <= COV < 40 % medium; COV >= 40 % high
High COV: more or different tests, judgment, or smaller less variable sub-sites
Table 5-14: unit weight 3-7 %, buoyant 0-10 %, phi' 2-13 %, su 13-40 %, su/sigma'vo 5-15 %
Table 5-14: SPT N 15-45 %, electric cone qc 5-15 %, mechanical cone 15-37 %, DMT 5-15 %, vane su 10-20 %
Statistics and sensitivity analyses are the minimum practice (GEC-5)
tables: Table 5-14: Coefficients of Variation for Geotechnical Properties and In-Situ Tests (after Duncan and Wright 2005) (p. 141)
sections.applicability: Assessing site variability for design parameter selection and resistance factors.

sections.title: Geotechnical Reporting
sections.summary: Three report types: geotechnical data report (5.6.1, factual only), foundation design report (5.6.2, assessment, parameters, analyses and recommendations for every limit state) and geotechnical baseline report (5.6.3, contractual baseline for risk allocation). Table 5-15 lists the pile decisions influenced by subsurface information; Table 5-16 the content of a data report.
sections.body: (p. 142) At the end of site characterization the geotechnical engineer prepares a report of one of three types, by project type and owner requirement: a geotechnical data report (5.6.1), a foundation design report (5.6.2) or a geotechnical baseline report (5.6.3). Data reports document the exploration and data and may serve design-bid-build or design-build; many agencies prefer design reports with an assessment and recommendations; baseline reports set a contractual understanding of expected conditions, uncommon on driven pile projects but growing on design-build projects with variable sites (Dwyre et al. 2010). Table 5-15 (printed in 5.6.1) lists the decisions the subsurface conditions influence.
key_points: Three report types: geotechnical data, foundation design and geotechnical baseline reports
Baseline reports are uncommon on driven pile projects but growing on variable design-build sites (Dwyre et al. 2010)
Table 5-15 (in 5.6.1): pile decisions influenced by subsurface information
sections.applicability: Geotechnical reporting requirements for driven pile foundation design and construction projects.

sections.title: Geotechnical Data Reports
sections.body: (pp. 142-144) A GDR holds only factual information: the geologic setting, the exploration and testing programs, final boring logs and field and laboratory results, with no interpretation or recommendation (Table 5-16, after Brown et al. 2010). It is typical where a subcontracted consultant explores for the foundation designer; the owner's design team interprets it, and on design-build projects it may be used for bidding and must be a contract document. Table 5-15 lists the decisions influenced by subsurface information: project constraints and auxiliary equipment, pile type and accessories, driving equipment, and construction control.
key_points: GDR: factual information only, no interpretation or design recommendations
Typical where a subcontracted consultant performs the exploration and testing
Owner's design team interprets the GDR; on design-build it may be a contract document for bidding
Table 5-15: constraints, pile type and accessories, driving equipment and construction control decisions
Table 5-16: background, scope of exploration and data presentation
tables: Table 5-15: Pile Foundation Decisions Influenced by Subsurface Information (p. 143)
Table 5-16: Information Included in Geotechnical Data Reports (after Brown et al. 2010) (p. 144)
sections.applicability: Contents and use of a geotechnical data report.

sections.title: Geotechnical Foundation Design Reports
sections.body: (pp. 144-148) A foundation design report presents the exploration, laboratory data, analyses and design and construction recommendations, with everything in Table 5-16 plus an assessment of conditions, stratigraphy, design parameters per layer, analyses and results; it should separate fact from interpretation and be clear, concise and accurate, as it is used through design, construction and claims. Preliminary recommendations sent with initial data are not a design report; the report must address axial compression and uplift, settlement, lateral resistance, seismic, scour and so on by limit state methods. Its parts (modified from Cheney and Chassie 2000): I table of contents; II introduction (factored loads, extreme events, performance criteria, hydraulics, site constraints); III scope of explorations; IV interpretation of subsurface conditions; V geomaterial design parameters; VI design procedures; VII conclusions and recommendations; VIII pile foundations (resistance type, unsuitable layers, pile types, toe elevations and lengths, minimum penetration per AASHTO 10.7.7, nominal compression, tension and lateral resistance, neutral plane and drag force, group settlement, test piles and load tests, resistance determination method per AASHTO Table 10.5.5.2.3-1, nominal driving resistance, preboring and toe reinforcement, driving requirements, cofferdams and seals, corrosion, effects on adjacent construction, obstructions, cobbles, groundwater); IX appendix graphics; X distribution to design, construction and maintenance engineers. On design-bid-build the report precedes final design and is cross-checked with drawings and special provisions; on design-build the team performs the final exploration and report.
key_points: Adds assessment, stratigraphy, parameters per layer, analyses and recommendations to the Table 5-16 data
Clearly distinguish factual from interpretive information
Must address axial, uplift, settlement, lateral, seismic and scour by limit state methods
Outline: I contents, II introduction, III explorations, IV interpretation, V parameters, VI procedures, VII conclusions
VIII pile foundations: types, lengths, minimum penetration, resistances, neutral plane, group settlement, tests, driving criteria
IX appendix graphics; X wide distribution to design, construction and maintenance engineers
Cross-check drawings, special provisions and report before final design documents are issued
sections.applicability: Contents of a geotechnical foundation design report for driven piles.

sections.title: Geotechnical Baseline Reports
sections.body: (p. 148) The GBR came from tunneling, where unexpected conditions quickly cost time and money. It is a single document setting the expected (or assumed) conditions contractually, so risk is allocated: conditions equal to or better than the baseline are the contractor's risk, worse ones the owner's. Baselines should be well defined, reasonable and realistic, derived from the exploration or local experience; a GBR is not a warranty but is the legal basis for differing site condition claims. Example: obstructions between EL 610 and EL 605, taken for baseline as reinforced concrete footing rubble up to 3 ft thick over 15 % of the Pier 4 footprint. Where both exist, a GBR takes precedence over a GDR (Essex 2007).
key_points: Single contractual statement of the subsurface conditions expected for construction
Conditions equal to or better than the baseline: contractor's risk; worse: owner's risk
Baselines well defined, reasonable and realistic; not a warranty; basis for differing site condition claims
A GBR takes precedence over a GDR in the contract document hierarchy (Essex 2007)
sections.applicability: Geotechnical baseline reports for risk allocation on driven pile projects.
